title: The economy is hot, but stocks are not.
detail:
The economy is hot, but stocks are not.
Nathan Bomey
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 4:03 PM CST 2 min read
^NDX
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The economy is hot, but stocks are not.

Why it matters: Concerns about the sustainability of the AI spending binge have been looming over Wall Street for months — and those haven't gone away just because Jensen Huang is back on the job.

State of play: AI stocks were down in the dumps again Wednesday despite signs of a humming economy, as the feverish embrace of Huang's return to Nvidia fades.

New data Wednesday showed the U.S. economy grew at a 4.3% annual rate in the third quarter, powered by business investment — far above the 3.4% originally reported.

And rapid growth looks set to continue in the fourth quarter, according to the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow estimate, Axios' Neil Irwin writes.

But those good vibes weren't enough to stave off another tech-led risk-off move in markets.

Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

By the numbers: The Nasdaq 100 index, which represents some of the biggest tech companies, was down as much as 4.7% Wednesday morning before closing down 0.6%.

It's now down nearly 12% since Huang was ousted (before he wasn't) at Nvidia.

Wednesday was another particularly ugly day for Nvidia, which closed down 3.9%.

The company has now shed nearly $1 trillion in market value since the Huang scandal broke and more than $2 trillion since its October peak.

Zoom in: The chip giant and center of the AI universe continues to face numerous unanswered questions surrounding the Huang episode.

And Wednesday, credit ratings firm S&P Global warned it may cut Nvidia's AA rating, citing concerns around its board's independence and "key man" risk.

Other AI stocks also swung between big losses and smaller ones Wednesday, with the chips sector and hyperscalers particularly volatile.

AMD, Micron, Intel and Marvell all pared far steeper losses before closing at 1.8%, 4.6%, 0.6% and 0.5%, respectively.

The Magnificent Seven were also feeling the pain Wednesday, with all but Meta and Apple trading down.

What they're saying: "We are not out of the woods with the downside risk from the AI trade, as the Jensen Huang stock put is fading," writes Chris Brigati, chief investment officer at San Antonio investment firm SWBC.

Investors are still nervous, he said. And fundamental questions about whether massive investments in AI will pay off remain unanswered.

Zoom out: Macro issues also contributed to Wednesday's stock volatility.

The federal government reported Wednesday that the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — rose 0.2% from September to 3.8% in October.

That likely heightens the chances of a Fed rate hike, putting additional pressure on growth stocks.

title: Michael Burry Bets on Stock Market Recovery After Thanksgiving
detail:
Michael Burry Bets on Stock Market Recovery After Thanksgiving
Lockridge Okoth
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 2:07 PM CST 3 min read
PLTR
^NDX
MET
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Michael Burry, the investor who famously predicted the 2008 housing market crash, is now betting on a stock market recovery.

On Wednesday, he revealed that he had closed his remaining bets against the Nasdaq 100, as the tech-heavy index briefly fell 20% from its October record high.

What Is Michael Burry Predicting Now?

In a Substack post, Burry revealed that he had taken profits from his bets on falling stock prices. Almost all his remaining investments are now positioned to benefit from rising prices.

He is still betting against two companies: Palantir and MetLife.

Michael Burry Stock Market Prediction

Around 25% of his portfolio remains in cash, which he is gradually looking to invest.

However, Burry made it clear that his bullish outlook is temporary.

"Right now apart from Palantir puts and MetLife puts, I am temporarily almost entirely long. Temporarily, because I am continuing to assess short opportunities."

His latest moves suggest he sees buying opportunities following the recent market crash. However, he has made no explicit prediction that the stock market has bottomed or that a sustained recovery is coming.

Days earlier, Burry also sold half of his bets against Nvidia before the chipmaker's shares rallied.

Why Are Stocks Falling the Day Before Thanksgiving?

The Trump administration proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China, the European Union, Japan, and India. Chinese goods face up to 20% on top of roughly 25% in existing duties.

Inflation added to the pressure. The PCE index, the Federal Reserve's preferred price gauge, rose 3.8% from a year earlier in October.

Traders now price a 97% chance of a Fed rate hike in December.

By 10 a.m. ET, the Nasdaq Composite was down about 4% and the S&P 500 about 2.7%.

Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 Performance. Source: TradingView

Nvidia fell 8% to roughly $141, with the move erasing more than half of Monday's 31% jump, which followed Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO.

Nvidia has lost $2 trillion in market value from its October peak.

Other chipmakers fared worse. SanDisk dropped 12% and Micron about 10%, while Ambarella plunged 25% after a weak forecast.

Together, the US stock market had wiped out over $1.7 trillion at market open.

The slide also breaks a holiday pattern. Since 1950, the S&P 500 has risen on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving in 58 of 76 years, Motley Fool data shows.

Investor Jeremy Lefebvre flagged the break from that pattern on X.

"The stock market almost NEVER crashes or even goes down the day before Thanksgiving. The fact this is occurring is a BAD OMEN. Even in 2018 the Nasdaq found a way to go up .9%," noted investor Jeremy Lefebvre.

detail:
Nasdaq 100 Flirts With Bear Market Territory, Drops 20% From October Highs
Shashank Nayar
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 11:53 AM CST 4 min read
^NDX
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nasdaq 100 on track for its first bear market since April 2025.

Nvidia alone drove roughly 23% of the drop amid turmoil surrounding CEO Jensen Huang.

Anthropic falling below its $83 IPO price weighed on market sentiment.

A wave of selling across artificial intelligence equities on Wednesday has sent the Nasdaq 100 tumbling toward its first bear market in more than a year.

The technology-heavy index dropped 4.7% in midday trade, bringing its decline from an all-time high set in early October to 20%. The pullback has wiped out more than $8.5 trillion in value and puts the benchmark on pace for its first bear market since the tariff-driven downturn in April 2025, leaving it down 0.6% for the year.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Investors have pulled back sharply from tech shares in recent weeks as doubts grow over the financial return on massive AI infrastructure spending. A tepid reception which sent the share prices of Anthropic below its listing price coupled with unease around multiple federal and congressional hearings pertaining to Nvidia's chip export practices have dampened sentiment.

Meanwhile, the greed and fear index dropped to the 'extreme fear' zone on Wednesday.

Greed and Fear Index As On November 25, 2026.
Chipmakers Bear The Brunt

Semiconductor stocks have absorbed the heaviest losses during the downturn. Nvidia (NVDA), Micron Technology (MU), Intel (INTC), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Lam Research (LRCX) and Applied Materials (AMAT) were the six largest drags on the Nasdaq 100 since its peak.

Combined, those six companies are responsible for more than 60% of the index's fall, Bloomberg data showed. Nvidia has stood out as the single biggest weight, accounting for roughly 23% of the drop on its own as shareholders react to abrupt executive upheaval involving CEO Jensen Huang.

Huang's removal unsettled the broader AI ecosystem, prompting investors to re-evaluate how shifting leadership could affect Nvidia's network of multibillion-dollar investments and financial commitments. Although his reinstatement sparked a 31% surge in Nvidia shares on Monday, sellers quickly regained control as broader headwinds persisted.

However, few market participants felt the sell off was overblown and the overall AI trade remains intact.

"All these fears are way overblown," Ross Gerber, co-founder at Gerber Kawasaki wrote in a post on X. "Think long term about the massive innovation happening in America."

Meanwhile, Mohammed El-Erian, chief economic advisor at Allianz said on Wednesday that he was cautiously buying technology stocks again. "I think that over the long term, this is going to be an opportunity," El-Erian told CNBC on Wednesday. "But I'm scaling in because I'm very, very conscious of the bad technicals. We are going to have margin calls left and right."
